title: Sound Doctrine and Abundant Mercy
summary: Paul charges Timothy to silence speculative teaching, defends the lawful use of the law, testifies to Christ’s mercy toward sinners, and urges a good warfare.
historicalContext: Paul writes after leaving Timothy in Ephesus while he himself travelled on into Macedonia, a movement that best fits the period of freedom between his first and second Roman imprisonments. Ephesus was the commercial and religious hub of the province of Asia, home to the great temple of Artemis, and the church there had already been warned that grievous wolves would rise from within its own ranks (Acts 20:29–30). By the time of this letter the warning had come true. Certain members, apparently with ambitions to lead, were absorbed in legends drawn from Jewish tradition, speculative genealogies, and arguments about the law that produced controversy without godliness. Timothy, younger than many he served and inclined to reserve, needed apostolic backing in writing, both to steady his own resolve and to show the congregation that his corrective work carried Paul’s authority under Christ.
literaryContext: The letter omits Paul’s customary thanksgiving and moves straight from greeting to commission, giving the opening chapter the tone of an official mandate addressed to a delegate. Two charges to Timothy frame the chapter (vv. 3–5 and 18–20). Inside that frame Paul sets the false teachers’ misuse of the law beside its rightful use, then turns to his own conversion as living proof of the gospel the law serves. The movement is deliberate: speculative religion breeds argument, the law rightly used exposes sin, the gospel of the blessed God answers sin with mercy, and that mercy erupts in a doxology before the apostle returns to the battle at hand. Themes introduced here—sound doctrine, a good conscience, faith and love, the trustworthy saying, and the peril of apostasy—recur throughout the letters to Timothy and Titus.
themes: Teaching measured by the apostolic gospel
Love as the goal of Christian instruction
The law’s goodness and its lawful use
Mercy that transforms the worst of sinners
Worship of the eternal, immortal King
Faith and conscience held together in spiritual warfare

outline.title: Apostolic Greeting to a True Son
outline.summary: Paul writes under God’s command to Timothy, his son in the faith, wishing him grace, mercy, and peace from the Father and the Son.

outline.title: A Charge Against Speculative Teaching
outline.summary: Timothy must stop teachers whose myths and genealogies breed disputes, for the goal of the apostolic charge is love from a pure heart, good conscience, and sincere faith.

outline.title: The Lawful Use of God’s Good Law
outline.summary: The law, which mirrors the Ten Commandments, rightly exposes and restrains sin and agrees with the sound teaching of the glorious gospel.

outline.title: Mercy to the Chief of Sinners
outline.summary: Paul thanks Christ for saving and commissioning a former persecutor, making him a pattern of divine patience, and bursts into praise of the eternal King.

outline.title: The Good Warfare and Shipwrecked Faith
outline.summary: Timothy is to fight faithfully, holding faith and a good conscience, warned by those who rejected conscience and came under corrective discipline.

verses.bibleText: Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the commandment of God our Saviour, and Lord Jesus Christ, which is our hope;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The letter opens in the conventional ancient form—writer, recipient, greeting—yet each element is filled with gospel content. Paul names himself “an apostle of Jesus Christ,” a title he holds by direct appointment from the risen Lord, not by election from any congregation (Galatians 1:1). Timothy hardly needed reminding of Paul’s office. The emphasis serves the church in Ephesus, which would hear this letter read aloud and needed to know that Timothy’s corrective work rested on an authority higher than his own age or temperament.

That authority is grounded “by the commandment of God.” Paul writes as a man under orders. His apostleship was a commission laid upon him, never a career he selected or a status he seized, and the same sense of obligation will shape the charge he passes to Timothy (vv. 3, 18).

Two titles stand out. God is “our Saviour,” language drawn from Israel’s worship, where the Lord repeatedly delivers His people (Psalm 25:5; Isaiah 45:21). In a city where rulers and patron deities were hailed as saviours, the Christian confession was pointed: deliverance comes from the living God alone. Elsewhere in these letters the same title is given to Christ (Titus 2:13), showing that Father and Son share fully in the work of redemption.

Christ Jesus is also called “our hope.” He is the substance of the believer’s future as well as the One who promises it. Biblical hope carries confident expectation, anchored in His resurrection and awaiting His appearing. The joining of God and Christ Jesus under one commandment, together with the shared pronoun “our,” places Paul, Timothy, and every believer under the same Lord and within the same expectation.

wordNotes.explanation: The word denotes an authoritative order or injunction. Paul uses it where he wants to stress that a directive comes from God rather than from human preference. Here it grounds his apostleship in a divine mandate, which in turn gives weight to the instructions Timothy must enforce in Ephesus.

In the New Testament hope is settled expectation of what God has promised, far removed from uncertain wishing. Calling Christ Jesus “our hope” identifies Him as both the ground and the content of the believer’s future, which will be fully realized at His return.

verses.bibleText: Unto Timothy, my own son in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace, from God our Father and Jesus Christ our Lord.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Timothy is addressed as Paul’s “own son in the faith.” The Greek adjective describes a child who is legitimate and true, one whose sonship is beyond dispute. Timothy probably came to faith through Paul’s preaching in Lystra (Acts 14:6–7; 16:1–3), and the years since had proved his loyalty; Paul could say that no one else shared his concern for the churches so fully (Philippians 2:20–22). Before a congregation unsettled by rival teachers, this description publicly confirms Timothy as a trustworthy bearer of the apostolic message.

The greeting expands Paul’s familiar “grace and peace” by placing “mercy” between them, a pattern found only in the letters to Timothy. Grace is God’s unearned favour that pardons and empowers; peace is the wholeness that follows reconciliation with God. Mercy adds His compassionate attention to human weakness and need. A young pastor facing opposition, frequent illness (5:23), and heavy responsibility would value the reminder that God bends toward the struggling.

All three gifts flow from a single source: “God our Father and Jesus Christ our Lord.” Paul places the Son beside the Father as the giver of divine blessing, a brief but unmistakable confession of Christ’s deity.

wordNotes.explanation: Gnēsios described a lawful child as distinct from an illegitimate one, and by extension anything authentic. Joined with teknon, a term of family affection, it marks Timothy as Paul’s true spiritual offspring, proven in service and fit to represent him.

Mercy is God’s compassion toward the wretched and helpless. In the Greek Old Testament the word often renders the Lord’s steadfast covenant love. Paul will soon describe his own conversion as an experience of this mercy (vv. 13, 16).

verses.bibleText: As I besought thee to abide still at Ephesus, when I went into Macedonia, that thou mightest charge some that they teach no other doctrine,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul recalls an earlier conversation. As the apostle set out for Macedonia, he “besought” Timothy to stay on in Ephesus. The verb can express a strong urging or an encouraging appeal, and both suit the setting. Timothy may well have preferred to travel with Paul; staying meant confronting difficult people in a demanding city without his mentor beside him. The sentence that begins here is never grammatically completed—Paul’s thought races ahead—yet the meaning is clear: Timothy is to remain at his post.

His task is to “charge some that they teach no other doctrine.” The verb for “charge” belongs to the vocabulary of command, used of orders passed down a line of authority. Timothy is no mere adviser offering suggestions. He carries a commission and is expected to exercise it.

Paul refers only to “some.” He does not name the offenders yet (that comes in v. 20), and he does not exaggerate the problem. The trouble lay with certain individuals, apparently within the congregation and perhaps among its leaders, as Paul had foreseen when he told the Ephesian elders that men would arise “of your own selves” speaking perverse things (Acts 20:30).

“Teach no other doctrine” translates a single verb meaning to teach something different. The phrase assumes that a recognizable body of apostolic teaching already existed, a standard against which any new instruction could be measured (Galatians 1:6–9). At issue is content rather than style. Teachers legitimately differ in gifts and emphasis, yet the substance of the gospel is closed to revision. Every generation feels the attraction of novelty in religion, and this verse draws a firm boundary: whatever departs from the faith once delivered to the saints is departure, however fresh it may sound.

wordNotes.explanation: This compound verb, found only here and in 6:3 in the New Testament, means to teach what differs from the apostolic standard. Paul uses the related idea of “another gospel” in Galatians, where difference amounts to contradiction of the truth received from Christ.
A verb of authoritative instruction, used of commands issued by a superior. It recurs throughout the letter, marking Timothy as a delegate whose directions carry apostolic weight in the congregation.

verses.bibleText: Neither give heed to fables and endless genealogies, which minister questions, rather than godly edifying which is in faith: so do.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The content of the rival teaching is now sketched. Its promoters gave close attention to “fables and endless genealogies.” The word for fables (mythoi) consistently describes stories with no basis in fact. Titus 1:14 calls such fables “Jewish,” and the false teachers wanted to be “teachers of the law” (v. 7), so the most likely background is the elaborate retelling of Old Testament history that flourished in some Jewish circles—imaginative expansions of the patriarchal narratives, lists of ancestors, and lines of descent loaded with supposed hidden meanings. Whether these were already blended with early Gnostic ideas is less certain. Paul’s concern lies less in cataloguing the error than in exposing its fruit.

The genealogies are “endless” because they never arrive anywhere. Speculation of this kind can always generate another question, another connection, another theory. So these pursuits “minister questions”—they breed disputes and investigations that feed curiosity and pride while leaving the conscience untouched.

Paul sets this against “godly edifying which is in faith.” The King James rendering follows manuscripts reading “edifying,” building up. Many early manuscripts read instead “God’s stewardship,” meaning the ordered plan by which God administers salvation and trains His household. Either reading yields the same essential contrast. One approach multiplies arguments; the other advances God’s work in human lives. That work is “in faith”: it is received and carried forward through trust in God’s revealed word, never through ingenuity that wanders beyond it.

The verse ends abruptly with “so do,” the implied conclusion of the sentence begun in verse 3. Timothy is to keep doing what Paul had urged. The warning remains timely wherever Bible study turns into a hunt for hidden codes or esoteric theories that inflame debate while producing little love, holiness, or trust. Any teaching may be tested by asking whether it builds God’s people up in faith.

wordNotes.term: μύθοις καὶ γενεαλογίαις (mythois kai genealogiais) — fables and genealogies
wordNotes.explanation: Mythoi refers to fictional tales presented as truth; in the New Testament it always carries a negative sense. Genealogiai are family lineages. Together they describe imaginative elaborations of biblical history that occupied the false teachers and generated controversy instead of faith.

Many manuscripts read oikonomia, the management of a household, where others read oikodomē, building up, the reading behind the King James Version. The first points to God’s saving arrangement and the training of His household through faith; the second to the strengthening of believers. Both stand opposed to speculation that only multiplies disputes.

verses.bibleText: Now the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Having described what the false teaching produces, Paul states what his own charge aims at. “The end of the commandment” refers first to the instruction Timothy is to deliver (v. 3), though the principle reaches to all apostolic teaching. “End” here means goal or intended outcome. The purpose of Christian instruction is love—“charity” in the older English sense of self-giving love that seeks the good of God and neighbour. Jesus summarized the law in the two great commandments of love (Matthew 22:37–40), and Paul calls love the fulfilling of the law (Romans 13:10). Teaching that leaves a church argumentative, proud, and divided has missed its purpose, however learned it appears.

Paul then traces love to three sources. Love grows “out of a pure heart.” In Scripture the heart is the center of the person—thought, desire, and will together. A pure heart is one cleansed by God and kept undivided in loyalty to Him (Psalm 51:10; Matthew 5:8). Love cannot flow freely from a heart still clutching resentment, ambition, or secret sin.

Love also springs from “a good conscience.” Conscience is the inner witness that evaluates conduct in light of what one knows of God’s will. A good conscience makes no claim to sinlessness; it belongs to someone who has confessed sin, received forgiveness through Christ, and walks honestly in the light (Hebrews 9:14; 10:22). Paul will soon warn that rejecting conscience leads to shipwreck (v. 19).

The third source is “faith unfeigned”—trust in God without pretence, free of the mask worn for religious performance. Hypocrisy will appear among the marks of the coming apostasy (4:2); sincere faith stands opposite it.

The order is instructive. Love is the fruit; the pure heart, good conscience, and sincere faith are the roots. Grace works from the inside outward. Doctrine matters precisely because true teaching about God, rightly received, purifies the heart, sets the conscience at rest, awakens trust, and so produces the love that marks Christ’s disciples (John 13:35). Measured by this goal, the speculative teachers stand exposed: their teaching yielded “questions” (v. 4) and no love.

wordNotes.explanation: Telos can mean termination, but here it denotes the goal toward which something is directed. The aim of apostolic instruction is love, the same end toward which God’s commandments have always pointed.

wordNotes.term: συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς (syneidēseōs agathēs) — a good conscience
wordNotes.explanation: Syneidēsis describes moral self-awareness, the inner faculty that approves or accuses one’s conduct. Paul joins a good conscience with faith three times in this letter (1:5, 19; 3:9), showing that sound belief and honest obedience cannot be separated. Christ’s cleansing makes such a conscience possible.

verses.bibleText: From which some having swerved have turned aside unto vain jangling;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Some in Ephesus had abandoned these three sources of love. “Having swerved” uses a verb meaning to miss the mark, like an archer whose arrow falls wide of the target. The same verb describes those who erred concerning the faith (6:21) and Hymenaeus with his companion, who missed the truth about the resurrection (2 Timothy 2:18). Having lost their aim, they “turned aside” into “vain jangling”—empty, futile talk.

The progression is sobering. The false teachers did not begin by announcing heresy. They drifted from purity of heart, honesty of conscience, and sincerity of faith, and their speech followed their inner condition. Talk became an end in itself, abundant in words and barren of fruit. Jesus warned that the mouth speaks out of the heart’s abundance (Matthew 12:34).

Religious conversation can become a substitute for obedience. A community can debate fine points with great energy while its love grows cold. The remedy is a return to the heart of the charge: a life cleansed by God, honest before Him, and trusting Him without pretence.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb pictures missing a target and so going astray. In the New Testament it appears only in the Pastoral Letters, each time of people who deviate from the truth, suggesting a gradual loss of direction more than a single dramatic act.
A compound of “empty” and “speech,” it describes talk that leads nowhere and accomplishes nothing for God. Titus 1:10 uses a related term for deceivers who are empty talkers.

verses.bibleText: Desiring to be teachers of the law; understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
These would-be teachers had an ambition: they were “desiring to be teachers of the law.” The term elsewhere describes respected Jewish experts in the law of Moses, such as Gamaliel (Acts 5:34; Luke 5:17). The Ephesian teachers wanted that kind of standing. Their interest in the law was real, but it served speculation and prestige instead of holiness.

Paul’s verdict is blunt. They understood “neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm.” They spoke with assurance, pressing their claims emphatically, yet they grasped neither their own statements nor the subjects they insisted upon. Confidence itself is no fault; Paul later wants Titus to “affirm constantly” the truths of the gospel, using the same verb (Titus 3:8). The fault is confidence detached from understanding.

The warning applies to anyone who teaches Scripture. James cautions that teachers will receive the stricter judgment (James 3:1). The desire to instruct others is honourable when it springs from love for God and His people and is joined to patient study, humility, and a life shaped by the truth. When it springs from a wish to be seen as an authority, it easily produces assertion without insight. Christ told the religious leaders of His day that they erred, knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God (Matthew 22:29). Command of terms and details cannot replace a grasp of what the law is for, and that is exactly what Paul now explains.

wordNotes.explanation: Used elsewhere of recognized Jewish scholars of the Mosaic law. Its use here indicates that the false teachers claimed expertise in the Old Testament law and built their speculative teaching upon it.
The verb means to assert strongly or insist confidently. Paul uses it approvingly of Titus’s teaching; here it exposes teachers who spoke with certainty about matters they did not understand.

verses.bibleText: But we know that the law is good, if a man use it lawfully;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul’s criticism of the would-be teachers must not be mistaken for criticism of the law itself. “But we know that the law is good.” The phrase “we know” appeals to settled Christian conviction. The law in view is God’s law given through Moses, and the list that follows shows that its moral heart, the Ten Commandments, stands at the center. Paul says the same in Romans: the law is holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good (Romans 7:12). The law reflects the character of the God who gave it.

The qualification is crucial: the law is good “if a man use it lawfully.” Paul makes a play on words—the law (nomos) must be used law-fittingly (nomimōs), in keeping with the purpose for which God gave it. An excellent tool can still be misused. The Ephesian teachers treated the law as raw material for myths, genealogies, and endless questions. Others in Paul’s day made it a ladder by which to climb into God’s favour (Galatians 2:16). Both distort it. The first drains the law of moral seriousness and turns it into a puzzle; the second robs grace of its glory.

Used lawfully, the law defines sin and exposes it (Romans 3:20; 7:7), drives the sinner to Christ for mercy (Galatians 3:24), restrains evil in society, and continues to describe the way of life that love produces (Romans 13:8–10). Faith does not make void the law; it establishes it (Romans 3:31). The gospel supplies what the law cannot—pardon and a new heart—so that the righteous requirement of the law is fulfilled in those who walk after the Spirit (Romans 8:3–4).

This verse sets a healthy balance for every age. Some treat God’s commandments as relics of a former era; others treat them as a means of earning salvation or as material for clever debate. Paul refuses all three. The law is good, permanent in its moral claims, and rightly honoured when it leads people to the Saviour and shapes the obedience of those He has redeemed.

wordNotes.explanation: Kalos describes what is excellent, fitting, and admirable in its function. The law is good because it comes from God and accomplishes the purpose for which He designed it.

The adverb means according to rule or in the proper manner. In 2 Timothy 2:5 it describes an athlete who competes by the rules. Here it insists that the law be used for its God-given purposes, never for speculation or self-justification.

verses.bibleText: Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners, for unholy and profane, for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, for manslayers,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“The law is not made for a righteous man.” Read in isolation, the sentence could be taken to mean that Christians have no further relation to God’s commandments. The context rules that out. Paul has just called the law good (v. 8), and he has not changed his mind between sentences. The verb “made” was a legal term for a law that is laid down against someone or applies to a case. The point is that the law’s threatening, restraining, and condemning work is aimed at wrongdoing. A person justified by faith and walking in obedience by the Spirit does not stand under its sentence (Romans 8:1). He delights in the law instead of chafing against it (Psalm 40:8; Romans 7:22). Far from being lawless, the righteous man is the very person in whom the law’s requirement is being fulfilled (Romans 8:4).

The law’s condemning edge falls on “the lawless and disobedient,” two general descriptions of those who reject God’s authority and refuse restraint. Then Paul begins a list that follows the order of the Ten Commandments. The first group describes violations of duty toward God: the “ungodly,” who have no reverence for Him; “sinners,” a term often used of those who turned from the true God to idols; the “unholy,” who treat the sacred, including God’s name, as common; and the “profane,” who trample on what God has set apart. The commandment that most directly calls something “holy” is the fourth, concerning the Sabbath day that God blessed and sanctified (Exodus 20:8–11). To profane what God has hallowed is to sin against the first table of the law.

The list then turns to duties toward others. “Murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers” may better be understood as those who strike or assault their parents, the gravest violation of the fifth commandment (Exodus 21:15). “Manslayers” are murderers, breakers of the sixth.

The extreme forms are chosen deliberately. Paul is showing that the law addresses real moral evil in concrete human conduct, a far cry from the speculative topics that absorbed the false teachers. The same law that exposes the parent-striker and the killer also searches every heart, and only the gospel can answer what it reveals.

wordNotes.explanation: Dikaios describes one who is upright, living in conformity to God’s will. Here it contrasts with the lawbreakers listed next. The law’s sentence is aimed at wrongdoing; the statement does not mean that the law ceases to guide those made righteous through faith in Christ.

The word describes what is common or unhallowed, open to all because it has been stripped of sacredness. Applied to people, it describes those who treat holy things as ordinary. Esau, who despised his birthright, is called profane, and Ezekiel rebukes priests who erased the difference between holy and profane and hid their eyes from God’s Sabbaths.

verses.bibleText: For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The list continues through the second table of the Decalogue. “Whoremongers” translates a broad term for sexual immorality, and “them that defile themselves with mankind” refers to men who engage in homosexual intercourse; Paul uses the same word in 1 Corinthians 6:9. Together they fall under the seventh commandment’s protection of marriage, reflecting the Creator’s design of male and female joined in covenant faithfulness (Genesis 2:24). In 1 Corinthians 6:11 Paul immediately adds that some believers had once lived this way but were washed, sanctified, and justified. Scripture names these sins precisely so that sinners may find cleansing.

“Menstealers” are kidnappers and slave-traders, people who seized human beings to sell them. The law of Moses made this a capital crime (Exodus 21:16; Deuteronomy 24:7), placing it under the eighth commandment as the theft of a person. In a Roman world economically dependent on slavery, Paul’s inclusion of the slave-dealer among the lawless is significant. The trade in human beings is condemned by the same law that forbids murder and adultery. Scripture’s trajectory, rooted in the dignity of every person made in God’s image, runs against the whole system of treating people as property.

“Liars” and “perjured persons,” those who break their sworn word, represent the ninth commandment. Truthfulness in speech, under oath or not, belongs to the law’s moral demand.

Paul closes with a sweeping clause: “and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine.” The list is representative, not exhaustive. More striking is the standard he names. The law and “sound doctrine” stand on the same side against these sins. “Sound” means healthy. Apostolic teaching is wholesome, producing moral and spiritual health, while sin is a disease that corrupts the whole person. False teaching, by implication, is sickly; Paul later compares it to gangrene that spreads (2 Timothy 2:17).

The gospel does not loosen the moral claims of the law. The healthy teaching of the church condemns the same evils the commandments forbid and offers the cure the law could only point toward.

wordNotes.explanation: The word denotes slave-dealers or kidnappers, those who captured free people and sold them. The Mosaic law punished such theft of persons with death. Its presence in this list places the traffic in human beings among the gravest violations of God’s law.

The participle means healthy or wholesome. This medical image, characteristic of the Pastoral Letters, presents apostolic teaching as health-giving truth in contrast with the diseased speculation of the false teachers.

verses.bibleText: According to the glorious gospel of the blessed God, which was committed to my trust.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The sound doctrine Paul has just named is measured “according to the glorious gospel of the blessed God.” The law’s moral standard and the gospel belong together. The gospel does not contradict the law’s verdict on sin; it supplies the answer to it. The false teachers isolated the law from the gospel and turned it into a field for speculation. Paul sets it back in its proper framework. The law exposes the disease; the gospel announces the cure.

The Greek reads more literally “the gospel of the glory of the blessed God.” The good news is the message that reveals God’s glory, His radiant goodness and saving character, displayed supremely in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:4–6). When Moses asked to see God’s glory, the Lord proclaimed His name as merciful, gracious, and longsuffering (Exodus 33:18–19; 34:6–7). The gospel brings that same glory to its fullest expression.

God is called “blessed,” a title applied to Him only here and in 6:15. The word speaks of His own perfect happiness and fullness. He needs no human worship to complete Him; He is the self-sufficient source of all good, who out of that fullness gives life and salvation.

Paul adds that this gospel “was committed to my trust.” He did not invent it or own it; it was entrusted to him as a steward (1 Corinthians 9:17; Galatians 2:7). That stewardship explains his urgency over the Ephesian error. Those entrusted with the gospel must guard it, proclaim it unaltered, and pass it on faithfully (6:20; 2 Timothy 2:2). The thought of that trust moves Paul to thanksgiving in the next verse.

wordNotes.term: τῆς δόξης τοῦ μακαρίου θεοῦ (tēs doxēs tou makariou theou) — of the glory of the blessed God
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase describes the gospel by its content: it makes known the glory of God. Makarios, used of God only here and in 6:15, describes His perfect blessedness, the fullness of life and joy within Himself.
The passive verb means “I was entrusted.” Paul regards the gospel as a deposit placed in his care by God, for which he is accountable as a steward.

verses.bibleText: And I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who hath enabled me, for that he counted me faithful, putting me into the ministry;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Mention of the gospel entrusted to him triggers an outburst of gratitude: “I thank Christ Jesus our Lord.” Paul’s thanksgiving rises from wonder, and three things in his call astonish him.

First, Christ “hath enabled me.” The verb means to strengthen or empower. Paul brought no natural fitness to his ministry; Christ supplied the strength the task required. The Lord who called him also sustained him, a conviction he voices elsewhere: “I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me” (Philippians 4:13).

Second, Christ “counted me faithful.” Paul did not earn his appointment by prior faithfulness, for the next verse describes how far from faithful he had been. Christ, knowing what grace would make of him, regarded him as one who could be trusted with a stewardship, and that confidence itself helped create the faithfulness it anticipated.

Third, Christ was “putting me into the ministry.” The word is diakonia, service. Paul’s apostleship, for all its authority, was a form of servanthood. He did not appoint himself; Christ placed him where he was to serve (Acts 26:16).

The verse holds a lesson for Timothy and for everyone in Christian service. Calling and capacity both come from Christ. A minister’s confidence rests on the Lord who enables, more than on temperament, education, or experience. Weakness is no disqualification when the One who calls also equips.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to strengthen or make able. Paul uses it of the power Christ supplies for faithful living and service, a power received from Him and never self-generated.
Diakonia means service, the work of one who acts on behalf of another. Paul repeatedly describes his apostolic labour with this term, presenting even high authority as service rendered under Christ.

verses.bibleText: Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now recalls what he had been before Christ met him, using three terms of mounting severity. He was “a blasphemer,” one who spoke against Christ and tried to compel believers to do the same (Acts 26:11). He was “a persecutor,” hunting down followers of Jesus, binding men and women and dragging them to prison (Acts 8:3; 22:4). And he was “injurious,” a word describing insolent violence, the arrogance that takes pleasure in wounding others. On the Damascus road Jesus identified Himself with His suffering people: “Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?” (Acts 9:4). Every blow Saul struck against the church had fallen on Christ.

“But I obtained mercy.” The passive verb points to God as the one who showed it. Paul did nothing to secure it; mercy reached him in the midst of his hostility.

He adds, “because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.” The clause does not claim that ignorance earned mercy or that his sins were slight, for he calls himself chief of sinners in verse 15. He is distinguishing his past from deliberate, high-handed rebellion against known light (Numbers 15:30–31) and from the hardened resistance to the Spirit that places a person beyond repentance (Matthew 12:31–32). Saul had acted with misguided zeal, convinced he was serving God (John 16:2; Acts 26:9). Once Christ revealed Himself, he was not disobedient to the heavenly vision (Acts 26:19). His ignorance was culpable—it sprang from unbelief—yet it had not hardened into knowing refusal.

The distinction carries both warning and comfort. Light brings responsibility; to reject clear truth from God is more serious than to sin in darkness (Luke 12:47–48; John 9:41). Yet no one who still responds to God’s drawing has gone too far for mercy. If the persecutor of the church could be forgiven, there is hope for anyone who turns to Christ.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun describes a violent, insolent person who mistreats others out of arrogance. Paul applies it to his former self, recognizing the cruelty of his campaign against the church.

Literally “I was shown mercy.” The passive voice stresses that mercy was God’s initiative toward one who deserved judgment. Paul repeats the verb in verse 16, making his experience a model of divine compassion.

verses.bibleText: And the grace of our Lord was exceeding abundant with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now describes the grace that met him: it “was exceeding abundant.” The verb is a compound intensified with “over,” meaning that grace overflowed beyond measure. Paul uses a similar expression in Romans 5:20: where sin abounded, grace did much more abound. The depth of his former sin only displayed the greater sufficiency of grace.

This overflowing grace came “with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.” Grace did not leave Saul as it found him. In place of unbelief (v. 13) came faith; in place of violent hatred came love. These are the fruits grace produces, evidence that God’s favour has taken hold of a life. Faith receives Christ, and love flows outward to God and to the very people Paul had once persecuted.

The phrase “in Christ Jesus” locates both faith and love in union with Christ. They are the life of Christ shared with Paul (Galatians 2:20), never virtues produced by self-reform. The link with verse 5 is plain: the love that is the goal of the charge flows from sincere faith, and Paul himself is the demonstration.

Grace is never rationed so that the worst sinners receive too little. Those most gravely wounded by sin find that God supplies grace in proportion to their need.

wordNotes.explanation: A compound verb found only here in the New Testament, combining “beyond” with “to be abundant.” It expresses grace that overflows every limit, more than sufficient for the greatest sin.
God’s unmerited favour, active and powerful, that forgives sin and transforms the sinner. Here grace is the source from which faith and love arise in a life that once lacked both.

verses.bibleText: This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Here Paul introduces the first of five “faithful sayings” in the Pastoral Letters (3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8). The formula marks a statement as trustworthy and widely recognized, probably a concise confession already familiar in the churches. This one is further described as “worthy of all acceptation”—deserving to be received fully and by everyone, without reservation.

The saying itself is the gospel in a sentence: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.” Each phrase carries weight. “Came into the world” implies that Christ existed before His human birth. He entered the world from the Father’s presence (John 1:1, 14; 16:28), and His incarnation was a mission undertaken by choice.

The purpose was “to save sinners.” Jesus described His own work in the same terms: the Son of man came to seek and to save that which was lost (Luke 19:10), and He came to call sinners to repentance (Luke 5:32). Salvation in Scripture is rescue from sin’s guilt, from its power, and finally from its wages, which is death (Romans 6:23). Those whom Christ saves receive eternal life as His gift instead of perishing.

The word “sinners” is the only qualification. Respectability, religion, and moral achievement bring no advantage, for the gospel is addressed to those who need saving. That wide scope will be stressed again in 2:4, where God wills all people to be saved.

Then Paul adds, “of whom I am chief.” He says “I am,” where he might have said “I was.” Years after his conversion, after missionary labours and suffering, he still regards himself as foremost among sinners. This is neither theatrical self-abasement nor a lapse in assurance. Paul speaks from a vivid memory of what he had done against Christ and His church (v. 13), and from a closer view of Christ’s holiness that made sin appear more grievous than ever. Those who draw nearest to Jesus see most clearly their own unworthiness and their daily need of His grace. Paul calls himself the least of the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:9) and less than the least of all saints (Ephesians 3:8).

Such humility guards the believer against spiritual pride, the very failing of the Ephesian teachers who wanted to be recognized authorities. A person who knows himself as the chief of sinners has no room to lord it over others or to treat the gospel as a platform for display. He can only marvel that Christ came for him.

wordNotes.term: πιστὸς ὁ λόγος (pistos ho logos) — this is a faithful saying
wordNotes.explanation: The formula, found only in the Pastoral Letters, introduces or endorses a reliable statement of Christian truth. It calls the hearer to place full confidence in the saying because it accords with God’s revealed gospel.

Prōtos means first, either in sequence or in rank. Paul uses it of rank: he regards himself as foremost among sinners. Verse 16 then plays on the sense of “first” as the leading example of Christ’s patience.

verses.bibleText: Howbeit for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first Jesus Christ might shew forth all longsuffering, for a pattern to them which should hereafter believe on him to life everlasting.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now explains why he received mercy, and the reason reaches beyond his own rescue: “that in me first Jesus Christ might shew forth all longsuffering.” The word “first” picks up “chief” from the previous verse. As the foremost of sinners, Paul became the foremost display of Christ’s patience. If the Lord could bear with a blasphemer and persecutor and transform him into an apostle, He can bear with anyone.

“Longsuffering” is patience under provocation, the slowness to anger that belongs to God’s revealed character (Exodus 34:6). Christ showed “all” of it, the full measure, in His dealings with Saul. He did not strike him down in his violence; He waited, pursued, and finally revealed Himself. That same patience still holds back judgment so that people may come to repentance (2 Peter 3:9, 15).

Paul’s conversion became “a pattern to them which should hereafter believe.” The word for pattern can describe an outline sketch or model that others follow. Paul’s story serves as a template for every later believer: the sinner, however hostile, meets the mercy of Christ, believes, and receives life. Each converted life since then becomes another illustration of the same patience.

The goal of that faith is “life everlasting.” Eternal life is God’s gift through Christ (Romans 6:23), received by faith and secure in Him now, and it will be fully bestowed when the dead in Christ are raised and the living are changed at His appearing (1 Corinthians 15:51–54). Human beings do not possess it by nature; it is given to those who believe on Him. This prospect, placed at the close of Paul’s testimony, lifts his thoughts toward the eternal King in the doxology that follows.

To believe “on him” is to rest one’s trust upon Christ as the foundation. Faith draws its security from the faithfulness of the One believed, whatever the strength of the one believing.

wordNotes.explanation: The word denotes patience that endures provocation for a long time without retaliating. In Scripture it is a characteristic of God, who delays judgment to give sinners opportunity to repent.

The noun means an outline, sketch, or model. Paul’s conversion functions as a representative example showing what Christ’s patience can accomplish in any believer. The same word describes the “form of sound words” Timothy must hold fast.

verses.bibleText: Now unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The recollection of mercy overflows into worship. Paul’s doxologies often break out when he contemplates the reach of God’s grace (Romans 11:33–36; Ephesians 3:20–21), and this one gathers four descriptions of God.

He is “the King eternal,” literally “the King of the ages.” His reign spans every era, past, present, and to come. Earthly rulers rise and fall; Rome’s emperors accepted divine honours, and one of them would soon order Paul’s death. The true King rules through all ages and will bring His kingdom to its consummation.

He is “immortal,” or incorruptible—beyond decay and death. This attribute belongs to God by nature, and later in the letter Paul states that God “only hath immortality” (6:16). Human beings are mortal and possess no undying soul by nature. Immortality comes to the redeemed as God’s gift, when the corruptible puts on incorruption at the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:53–54). The life everlasting promised in verse 16 depends on union with the only One who has life in Himself.

He is “invisible.” No human eye can look upon God in His essential glory (John 1:18; 1 Timothy 6:16), yet He has made Himself known in His Son, who is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15).

He is “the only wise God.” Many manuscripts read simply “the only God”; either way the emphasis falls on God’s uniqueness. Against the crowded pantheon of Ephesus, Paul confesses one God without rival.

To Him belong “honour and glory for ever and ever.” The fitting response to such a God is reverent worship and grateful praise. Doctrine that rightly understands mercy ends in adoration, the very opposite of the barren disputes Paul has been confronting.

wordNotes.term: βασιλεῖ τῶν αἰώνων (basilei tōn aiōnōn) — King eternal
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “King of the ages,” a Hebrew-style expression for God’s everlasting rule over all time. It echoes Old Testament praise of the Lord as the everlasting King whose dominion endures through all generations.

The adjective means incorruptible, not subject to decay. God possesses this quality inherently. The same word describes the resurrection state of the redeemed and the inheritance reserved for them, showing that incorruption is a gift God grants, not a natural human possession.

verses.bibleText: This charge I commit unto thee, son Timothy, according to the prophecies which went before on thee, that thou by them mightest war a good warfare;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul returns to the charge with which the chapter began (vv. 3–5). “This charge I commit unto thee, son Timothy.” The verb means to entrust something to another for safekeeping, and the same verb appears when Timothy is told to commit the truth to faithful men who will teach others (2 Timothy 2:2). The commission passes from Christ to Paul, from Paul to Timothy, and from Timothy to the next generation.

The charge accords with “the prophecies which went before on thee.” At the outset of Timothy’s ministry prophetic words had been spoken about him, probably when the elders laid hands on him (4:14). Just as the Spirit had spoken through prophets at Antioch to set apart Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:1–3), so God had marked Timothy for His service. These words carried more weight than human compliments; they expressed God’s choice.

Timothy is to draw strength “by them.” In moments of discouragement he can recall that his calling came from God and was recognized by the church. That memory would steady him against opponents and against his own hesitancy.

The purpose is that he “might war a good warfare.” The image is military: Timothy is a soldier on campaign, under orders from his Commander (2 Timothy 2:3–4). The warfare is “good” because it is noble and fought on God’s side in the great conflict between Christ and the powers of evil (Ephesians 6:12). Ministry involves struggle against error, against sin, and against the spiritual forces that oppose the gospel. It demands endurance, discipline, and loyalty, while the outcome rests with the Lord who calls.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun refers to a military campaign or a soldier’s service. Paul uses military language for the Christian life and ministry, emphasizing discipline, endurance, and allegiance to Christ as Commander.
Prophecy in the New Testament is communication from God through those gifted by the Spirit. Here the plural refers to inspired utterances that pointed to Timothy and confirmed his call to ministry.

verses.bibleText: Holding faith, and a good conscience; which some having put away concerning faith have made shipwreck:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The good warfare is fought by “holding faith, and a good conscience.” Paul names two essentials, both introduced already in verse 5. Faith clings to God and the truth He has revealed; a good conscience keeps the life in step with that truth. Belief and behaviour are inseparable. Faith without conscience becomes hollow profession, and conscience without faith lacks the anchor of God’s word.

Some had “put away” conscience. The verb is strong, meaning to thrust aside or reject deliberately. These people silenced conscience; they did not merely misplace it. The result was that “concerning faith” they “made shipwreck.” Paul, who had himself survived shipwreck more than once (2 Corinthians 11:25; Acts 27:41–44), uses a vivid picture: a vessel that abandons rudder and compass is soon driven onto the rocks.

The sequence is a warning. Moral compromise rarely stays moral. When a person persists in violating conscience, conviction weakens, and doctrinal error eventually follows to justify the life. Guarding the conscience through daily obedience and confession is a safeguard for faith itself.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to push away or repudiate. It describes a deliberate rejection, as when Israel thrust Moses aside or the Jews of Pisidian Antioch put the word of God from them.
Literally “suffered shipwreck.” Paul uses it figuratively for the ruin of faith that follows when conscience is abandoned and the believer drifts from the truth once received.

verses.bibleText: Of whom is Hymenaeus and Alexander; whom I have delivered unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul names two who had made shipwreck: “Hymenaeus and Alexander.” Hymenaeus reappears in 2 Timothy 2:17–18, where he and Philetus teach that the resurrection is already past, an error that overthrew the faith of some. To deny a future bodily resurrection severs Christian hope from Christ’s return, when the dead in Christ will rise (1 Thessalonians 4:16). Alexander may be the coppersmith of 2 Timothy 4:14 who did Paul much harm, though the name was common and certainty is impossible.

Paul says, “whom I have delivered unto Satan.” The same expression appears in 1 Corinthians 5:5, where the congregation is told to remove an unrepentant member from its fellowship. Delivering someone to Satan describes formal exclusion from the church. Scripture recognizes two realms in the great controversy: the kingdom of God’s dear Son and the power of darkness (Colossians 1:13). A person who persistently rejects the faith has already chosen the side he serves; the church’s action acknowledges that choice and withdraws its fellowship.

The purpose is remedial: “that they may learn not to blaspheme.” The verb for “learn” means to be trained or disciplined, as a child is. Exclusion was intended to bring the offenders to their senses, awaken them to the seriousness of their condition, and lead them to repentance. Paul elsewhere hopes that discipline will result in salvation in the day of the Lord (1 Corinthians 5:5) and urges that the corrected be restored and comforted (2 Corinthians 2:6–8; Galatians 6:1).

“Blaspheme” here refers to teaching and conduct that dishonoured God and misrepresented His truth. Paul himself had once been a blasphemer (v. 13) and had received mercy; his hope for these men reflects that experience.

Church discipline, rightly practised, protects the flock and seeks the good of the erring. Harshness forgets its restorative aim; neglect forgets the seriousness of sin. Paul holds both together: firm action for the sake of the truth, and hope for those who have wandered.

wordNotes.term: παρέδωκα τῷ Σατανᾷ (paredōka tō Satana) — delivered unto Satan
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase describes removing a person from the church’s fellowship and so placing him outside the visible community of Christ, in the realm where Satan holds sway. Its intent, as in Corinth, was correction and eventual restoration.
The verb paideuō means to train, instruct, or discipline, especially of a child. Its use shows that the exclusion was meant as corrective instruction, leaving the door open to repentance.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: How can a church tell whether its Bible teaching is producing what God intends?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Apostolic teaching aims at love from a pure heart, uses God’s good law rightly, and centers on Christ who came to save sinners; faith and a good conscience must be held together to the end.
discussionQuestions: What marks distinguish teaching that builds faith from teaching that only multiplies questions?
Why does Paul insist that the law is good while rebuking those who wanted to be its teachers?
How does the list in verses 9–10 follow the Ten Commandments, and what does that reveal about the law’s continuing role?
Why does Paul say “I am chief” rather than “I was chief” of sinners?
In what ways does the discipline described in verse 20 aim at restoration?
commonMisunderstandings: “The law is not made for a righteous man” does not release Christians from the Ten Commandments; the law’s sentence targets wrongdoing, while the justified delight to obey it.
Paul’s ignorance did not earn mercy; it distinguished his sin from deliberate, hardened rejection of known light.
Being “delivered unto Satan” is corrective church discipline that hopes for repentance, not a curse pronounced over a lost soul.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep law and gospel in their God-given relationship: the law exposes sin and describes righteousness, while the gospel of the blessed God brings mercy that produces faith, love, and a good conscience.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Receive the faithful saying for yourself, guard your conscience by daily obedience, and let the mercy shown to the chief of sinners make you patient with others and steadfast in the good warfare.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and His patience with the worst of them proves that no one who turns to Him lies beyond mercy.
flow: God’s good law reveals the reality and seriousness of sin.
No moral record or religious knowledge can remove that guilt.
Christ Jesus entered the world for the express purpose of saving sinners.
His mercy toward Paul displays the patience He extends to every sinner who believes.
Those who receive Him are given everlasting life and a renewed heart that loves His law.
simpleIllustrations: A doctor’s diagnosis is valuable because it sends the patient to the cure; the law diagnoses sin so that sinners will seek Christ.
A ship that throws its compass overboard may sail calmly for a while, but the rocks are certain; a conscience guided by God’s word keeps faith on course.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you accept the faithful saying that Christ came to save sinners and receive His mercy for yourself today?
cautions: Do not suggest that the gospel cancels the moral law; it removes condemnation and empowers obedience.
Do not present Paul’s past as so extraordinary that ordinary sinners conclude they need little mercy.
Do not use the list of sins in verses 9–10 to single out particular groups while ignoring everyone’s need of grace.

reflectionQuestions: Does my study of Scripture produce more love in me, or more argument?
Where might I be using God’s law to win debates instead of letting it search my own heart?
Do I still see myself as someone who needs mercy every day, or have I begun to treat grace as something I needed long ago?
Is there any area of my life where I am pushing aside the voice of conscience?
How should the patience Christ has shown me shape the way I treat those who have wandered?
